analysis.one_liner: Repeals the health reform rule that lets adult children stay on a parent's health insurance until age 26.
analysis.headline: The bill, which had no cosponsors, died in the Energy and Commerce Committee without a vote, and the rule letting adult children stay on a parent's insurance until 26 remained in force.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have deleted one specific part of the 2010 health care law: the requirement that health plans covering dependents must keep a child covered on a parent's plan until the child turns 26. Repealing it would mean adult children under 26 could again be pushed off their parents' insurance, ending one of the most widely used provisions of the health reform law. The bill was introduced days after the 2010 election and received no cosponsors.
analysis.who_benefits: If the bill had passed, health insurers and large employers would gain the most: they could stop covering young adult children on family policies, cutting enrollment of a group that uses significant medical care (childbirth, injuries, chronic conditions). Parents of adult children who prefer not to pay for that coverage would also save on premiums. Young adults themselves would lose guaranteed access to a parent's plan, and many would end up uninsured or paying for separate individual policies.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Health insurers and employers' benefits budgets

how_it_helps.text: It repeals the ACA requirement that group health plans and insurers offering group or individual coverage keep dependent coverage available until an adult child turns 26.
The repeal is effective on the date of enactment, so insurers could stop offering dependent coverage to young adults immediately upon passage.

analysis.who_pays: Young adults under 26 who would lose the right to stay on a parent's plan, plus their parents and families, who would face either the cost of separate coverage or the risk of going uninsured.
analysis.who_pays_short: Young adults under 26 and their families

drawbacks.text: The bill would strip young adults up to age 26 of guaranteed access to a parent's health plan, a protection that helped roughly 2.5 million young people gain coverage after the ACA took effect (general knowledge about the provision's reach); many would lose coverage entirely or pay for separate, more expensive individual policies.

It would shift costs back to families, since parents would either go without coverage for their adult children or buy a separate family plan, and it would restore pre-ACA barriers such as plan rules that denied coverage to young adults who had an offer of insurance through their own employer (general knowledge about pre-2010 dependent-coverage rules).
Repealing the mandate effective immediately on enactment would leave plans free to drop currently covered young adults at the next renewal, with no transition.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's benefit runs entirely to insurers and parents of adult children who no longer pay for a young adult's policy; its cost falls on young adults, the group with the highest uninsured rate in the country, and on families who would absorb the cost of separate coverage. There is no compensating public benefit in the bill text: it repeals the provision outright with no replacement mechanism, so the drawbacks outweigh any benefit. Because it never advanced, no cost was imposed.

outcome.mechanism: It never got past its referral to committee: with no cosponsors and a Congress that ended days later, nobody called it up, and it died without a vote.

narrative.text: Rep. Ackerman introduced the bill on November 29, 2010, and it was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce the same day.
No member of the House signed on as a cosponsor.
The action history shows no committee markup, no hearing, no floor vote, and no further action of any kind after the referral.
The bill would have repealed the ACA provision (section 2714(a) of the Public Health Service Act) requiring plans that offer dependent coverage to keep it available until a child turns 26.
The 111th Congress ended on January 3, 2011, and all bills not enacted die with it.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Young adults and their families are better off, because the under-26 coverage guarantee they rely on stayed in force. Health insurers also gained nothing they could act on, but they lost nothing either, since the status quo kept the mandate in place.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Young adults still covered under age 26

for.name: Rep. Gary Ackerman
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on November 29, 2010 to repeal the ACA's under-26 dependent coverage requirement; it was his lone sponsorship, with no cosponsors joining.

against.name: House Committee on Energy and Commerce
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral on November 29, 2010 and took no further action — no markup, no hearing, no vote — before the Congress ended.

against.name: All 433 other House members
against.what_they_did: None signed on as a cosponsor, leaving the bill with zero support in the chamber.

sides.party_line_note: The bill came from a single Democrat with zero cosponsors of either party, so no party bloc ever took a position on it.

industries.note: Repealing the under-26 mandate would let insurers drop young adults from family policies and end required coverage for an age group with significant medical needs, cutting claims costs. The industry's gain comes directly at the expense of the young adults and families who would lose the coverage guarantee, so its interest runs against the public in this bill.

industries.industry: Large employers that sponsor health plans
industries.note: Employers offering group coverage could stop paying premiums for employees' adult children, reducing benefits costs. The savings would come out of coverage for employees' children.
